quote: And so Keats, with Charles Lamb and William Wordsworth and Benjamin Haydon, drank “confusion to the memory of Newton” because “he destroyed the poetry of the rainbow by reducing it to a prism.” That’s one reason to suspect Keats didn’t understand the subject too deeply.
content: The story is from Haydon’s Autobiography account of the “Immortal Dinner” of 28 December 1817, written decades later, and it does not say what the essay says. In Haydon’s telling, it was Lamb, drunk, who abused Haydon for putting Newton’s head in his painting, said Newton “had destroyed all the poetry of the rainbow by reducing it to the prismatic colours,” and proposed the toast; Keats “agreed”; and Wordsworth, the target of Lamb’s teasing, was the poet who had written of Newton’s statue as “the marble index of a mind for ever / Voyaging through strange seas of Thought, alone” (The Prelude, III). The essay’s further guess, that Keats “could not have sketched out on paper why rainbows only appear when the Sun is behind your head,” is a guess about a man who had completed a medical apprenticeship, passed the Apothecaries’ examination in 1816 after a course at Guy’s Hospital that included chemistry, and whose surviving medical notebook shows him a competent student of the science of his day (Goellnicht, The Poet-Physician: Keats and Medical Science, 1984; Holmes, The Age of Wonder, 2008, books with no DOI). Keats knew more optics than most poets and chose the Romantic side of the argument anyway, which is a more interesting fact than the one the essay invents, and is inconvenient for its thesis that anti-reductionism is a symptom of not having understood.

quote: —which was actually known in the thirteenth century. Newton only added a refinement by showing that the light was decomposed into colored parts, rather than transformed in color.
content: The century is wrong and the history omits the person who answered the two questions the essay says Keats could not. The explanation of the rainbow by refraction and internal reflection within individual drops is due to Theodoric of Freiberg (c. 1304–1310) and, independently, Kamal al-Din al-Farisi in Persia (c. 1300), both in the fourteenth century, not the thirteenth; and it was Descartes, in Les Météores (1637), who computed by ray-tracing that the primary bow appears at about 42° from the antisolar point, which is why it is an arc of a circle and why the Sun must be behind the observer. Newton’s contribution was dispersion, as the essay says. Boyer’s The Rainbow: From Myth to Mathematics (1959, a book with no DOI) is the standard history. The point is small in itself, but the essay is a lecture on the difference between knowing the woof and texture of the rainbow and merely having heard that it was explained, and it gets the woof and texture wrong in the one paragraph where it offers them.

quote: I think this distinction probably accounts for a hell of a lot of the deadly existential emptiness that supposedly accompanies scientific reductionism.
content: The positive half of this is testable, and the tests favour it. Models of aesthetic experience in empirical aesthetics find that understanding generally deepens appreciation rather than flattening it (Leder et al. (2004)); science-elicited awe is a measurable emotional state with the same profile as awe at nature (Keltner & Haidt (2003)), and “Science is awe-some” (Valdesolo, Shtulman & Baron (2017)) reviews evidence that the experience of scientific explanation recruits awe and that awe in turn promotes interest in explanation. So the claim that a person who sees how the rainbow works is not impoverished by it is well supported, and the essay is right to insist on the difference between seeing and being told. The negative half, that anti-reductionists feel empty because all they have is the password “Science,” is a claim about other people’s inner states supported by the essay’s inference about Keats, which the annotation above found to be false. The mechanism may still be common; the essay has not shown it in the one case it examined.
